newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: NZ's Peters appeals for support for new pensions.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters appeals for support for new pensions.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters appealed on Monday for support for his plans for a compulsory superannuation scheme to cover all pensioners.

The newly-installed New Zealand government will hold a referendum in September to ask for approval for a new pension system which would force all New Zealanders eventually to save at least eight percent of their income.

Peters, who met senior officials of Singapore's Central Provident Fund (CPF) compulsory savings scheme earlier on Monday, said a new pension system was essential if old people were to be covered adequately at retirement.
"What's wrong with the current system is that it is not sustainable," Peters told reporters. "We have the same ageing population that other countries have."
"By 2030 we will about 2.7 workers for every superanuator. I don't think any person thinks that is going to be, on the present level of expenditure, a sustanable situation," he added.

If the plan is approved it will come into force on July 1, 1998 with employees contributing three percent of their income to a fund. This would be matched by a three percent tax cut. Later, savings rates would be raised to eight percent, he said.
Peters said he intended to get approval for the scheme, which was being worked out by a government Design Team.
"If the answer is in the negative, the day after we will have all the same problems. But we are not thinking of losing."
"The system which we are obliged to design will be the best possible system for the New Zealand people. One of its features will be its sustainability," he said.

He said his government was considering a number of saving models from around the world but liked the Singapore system because it increased savings ratios. He said he believed New Zealand's savings ratios were not high enough.

"I personally believe that one of the critical determinants of Singapore's success has been their national savings rate," he said. "We are looking at Singapore. We are looking all around the world so that we might design the best possible option."

Under Singapore's CPF system, employees contribute 20 percent of their gross income to a government-administered savings account and employers then match that sum, bringing total savings to 40 percent of gross income.
Employees can then use the money for their retirement, as well as for house purchases.
Peters, leader of the New Zealand First party, which is part of a coalition government with the National Party, declined to say which particular aspects of the CPF system he liked.
He said there might be a lead time of a year for businesses to adapt to the scheme.
Peters said people who were already saving a large proportion of their income in existing schemes might be exempt from any compulsory scheme.
